title: Dizzy shows him bebop harmonies; Cab bans it
summary: After the firing Diz practised intensively and raved about Charlie Parker's chord substitutions; when both tried the ideas on "Some of These Days" Cab threatened to fire them, so Jones stuck to his commercial style, as he had a family.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: Well, that's when he went into the woodshed. That's when he went in to practice, and he was already getting together with bebop.

He'd already heard Charlie and he was raving and everything about this guy that runs the G-minor 7th against a C 7th, and that gives you your flatted fifth, your flatted seventh, your flatted ninth, and all that, you know. Because he was there telling me all of this, you know? He

was telling me this when he come back raving. And we were pretty good pals, you know, in the band. And he was raving about this, and we said, "What can it be?" We'd never heard of the thing. "Yeah, but this guy is playing something else." So now he's telling me all about it. He was trying to show me how it goes, and I said, "Yeah, but like two and two is four, you know." And he said, "No, not exactly." So now he gets enough nerve to get up on the stand, and he had a chorus of "Some of These Days," and so he gets up there and he makes the thing, and it sounded real funny in those days on the trumpet, because it wasn't being played. (Singing). And Cab said, "What the hell is that?" He said, "Don't make that in my band. Don't play that, whatever it is. I don't want to hear that." He said, "Give that part to Jonah," you know. So now he's down there and he says okay, and so he gives it to me, you know. There wasn't no hard feelings. So he gives it to me and I started playing it, and all at the same time Dizzy's showing me this thing. He's so insistent about this, you know. He's down there and he's got Milt [Hinton] playing the bass between shows, and because the bass and everything's got to go along with it, you know, and the rhythm, you know. And Danny, he wasn't practicing between shows, and Benny Payne, he wasn't going to practice between shows. But Milt would practice with him between shows, you know. And he's getting this thing together. He didn't care, because -- but I was there and I

wanted to see what he was doing, you know. Anyhow, we always walked around together between shows. So now he's showing it to me, and he says, "Jonah, you see this? And if you get here and you've got this chord going too long, just sit there playing the straight F chord. Play that chord one bar. You've got four bars after it, then go to F-sharp and come back to F again, you know." And I said, "Yeah, it's interesting." So I get on the stand with "Some of These Days," and I made one of these things, and Cab said, "You too?" He said, "I'm going to fire both of you." He said, "I'm going to fire both of you, playing that. I won't have that in my band." So I said, "I better stay away from this." Because you began to think about it, you know. You began to think, well, maybe this is something, you know what I mean? And sure enough, here comes a guy, bebop records, and here comes the opening of the Bebop Club, you know, on 49th Street. So, well, maybe this is a thing here. But I said, no, I've always been pretty sensible about where I'm going. I've been commercially thinking. I think I've been a little bit commercially thinking all along, you know. And one reason I had to do it was because I had a family, you know. So I went on back to playing my old way, you know. And you had to do that in Cab's band, because he kept you in that mold, you know. Now, like you couldn't do with Stuff, you know, start out taking all them choruses and things. Many a night I sat up there and played 25 choruses,
